steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Use on other operating systems" section of a Wikipedia article on the APK file format, covering the non-Android operating systems that have supported running or sideloading Android apps.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- BlackBerry 10
- Windows 10 Mobile: Astoria / Windows Bridge for Android, and its cancellation
- HarmonyOS
- Windows 11: Windows Subsystem for Android

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- BlackBerry 10
  - QNX-based; included Android runtime environment
  - at first apps had to be packaged in the OS's native format; installed via BlackBerry World app store or sideloading
  - from BlackBerry 10.2.1: sideloading APK files directly supported
- Windows 10 Mobile / Astoria
  - Build 2015: Microsoft announces Android runtime environment codenamed "Astoria", later renamed Windows Bridge for Android
  - Android apps run in emulated environment with minimal changes
  - access to Microsoft platform APIs (Bing Maps, Xbox Live) as nearly drop-in replacements for equivalent Google Mobile Services
  - no Google Mobile Services, certain core APIs missing; apps with "deep integration into background tasks" said to poorly support it
  - delayed November 2015; shelved February 25, 2016
  - focus instead on Windows Bridge for iOS (native implementation of iOS Objective-C APIs; Xcode projects -> Visual Studio projects targeting Windows platforms) and cross-platform development with C#
  - portions of Astoria used as basis for Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) on PC version of Windows 10
- HarmonyOS
  - August 9, 2019: APK compatibility via AOSP base with Linux kernel, HarmonyOS 1.0 for TVs
  - June 2, 2021: HarmonyOS 2.0 expanded to smartphones and tablets
  - until Galaxy Edition under HarmonyOS NEXT, next iterative HarmonyOS 5 beta to commercial version
  - November 26, 2024 stable: APK support officially dropped
- Windows 11 / WSA
  - June 2021: Microsoft announces "Windows Subsystem for Android" (WSA), AOSP-based layer for sideloading Android apps on Windows 11
  - runtime compiler developed by Intel
  - apps sideloaded, published via Microsoft Store, or from an Amazon Appstore client
  - deprecated and discontinued March 2025

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The BlackBerry 10 operating system, which is based on QNX, included an Android runtime environment. At first, apps had to be packaged in the operating system's own native format and then installed through the BlackBerry World app store or by sideloading. Starting with BlackBerry 10.2.1, the operating system also added support for sideloading APK files directly.

Microsoft announced at Build 2015 an Android runtime environment for Windows 10 Mobile, codenamed "Astoria" and later renamed Windows Bridge for Android. It would let Android apps run in an emulated environment with minimal changes, and the apps would have access to Microsoft platform APIs like Bing Maps and Xbox Live, which would be nearly drop-in replacements for the equivalent Google Mobile Services. Google Mobile Services and some core APIs would not be available, and apps that had "deep integration into background tasks" were said to poorly support the environment. Microsoft had already delayed it in November 2015, and on February 25, 2016 Microsoft announced that Windows Bridge for Android would be shelved. Instead Microsoft would focus on Windows Bridge for iOS (a native implementation of the iOS Objective-C APIs, which lets Xcode projects be converted to Visual Studio projects targeting Windows platforms) and on cross-platform development using the C# language. Portions of Astoria were then used as a basis for Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) on the PC version of Windows 10.

- HarmonyOS: August 9, 2019, APK compatibility via AOSP base with Linux kernel, HarmonyOS 1.0 for TVs; June 2, 2021 HarmonyOS 2.0 expanded to smartphones and tablets; until Galaxy Edition under HarmonyOS NEXT (HarmonyOS 5 beta to commercial); November 26, 2024 stable, APK support officially dropped
- June 2021: Windows Subsystem for Android (WSA), AOSP-based layer for sideloading Android apps on Windows 11; Intel runtime compiler; sideloaded, Microsoft Store, or Amazon Appstore client; deprecated and discontinued March 2025

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The BlackBerry 10 operating system, which is based on QNX, included an Android runtime environment. At first, apps had to be packaged in the operating system's own native format and then installed through the BlackBerry World app store or by sideloading. Starting with BlackBerry 10.2.1, the operating system also added support for sideloading APK files directly.

Microsoft announced at Build 2015 an Android runtime environment for Windows 10 Mobile, codenamed "Astoria" and later renamed Windows Bridge for Android. It would let Android apps run in an emulated environment with minimal changes, and the apps would have access to Microsoft platform APIs like Bing Maps and Xbox Live, which would be nearly drop-in replacements for the equivalent Google Mobile Services. Google Mobile Services and some core APIs would not be available, and apps that had "deep integration into background tasks" were said to poorly support the environment. Microsoft had already delayed it in November 2015, and on February 25, 2016 Microsoft announced that Windows Bridge for Android would be shelved. Instead Microsoft would focus on Windows Bridge for iOS (a native implementation of the iOS Objective-C APIs, which lets Xcode projects be converted to Visual Studio projects targeting Windows platforms) and on cross-platform development using the C# language. Portions of Astoria were then used as a basis for Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) on the PC version of Windows 10.

HarmonyOS came with APK compatibility on August 9, 2019, through an AOSP base with Linux kernel, on HarmonyOS 1.0 for TVs. On June 2, 2021, the HarmonyOS 2.0 version expanded this to smartphones and tablets. That lasted until the Galaxy Edition version under the HarmonyOS NEXT system, for the next iterative HarmonyOS 5 going from beta to commercial version, and starting with the November 26, 2024 stable release APK support was officially dropped.

In June 2021 Microsoft announced the "Windows Subsystem for Android" (WSA). This was an AOSP-based layer for sideloading Android apps on Windows 11. It used a runtime compiler that was developed by Intel, and apps could be sideloaded, published through the Microsoft Store, or gotten through an Amazon Appstore client. Microsoft deprecated and discontinued WSA in March 2025.

The BlackBerry 10 operating system, which is based on QNX, included an Android runtime environment. It would let Android apps run in an emulated environment with minimal changes, and the apps would have access to Microsoft platform APIs like Bing Maps and Xbox Live, which would be nearly drop-in replacements for the equivalent Google Mobile Services. Google Mobile Services and some core APIs would not be available, and apps that had "deep integration into background tasks" were said to poorly support the environment.[4,5] Microsoft had already delayed it in November 2015,[6,7] and on February 25, 2016 Microsoft announced that Windows Bridge for Android would be shelved. Instead Microsoft would focus on Windows Bridge for iOS (a native implementation of the iOS Objective-C APIs, which lets Xcode projects be converted to Visual Studio projects targeting Windows platforms) and on cross-platform development using the C# language.[8,9] Portions of Astoria were then used as a basis for Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) on the PC version of Windows 10.[10]

In June 2021 Microsoft announced the "Windows Subsystem for Android" (WSA). This was an AOSP-based layer for sideloading Android apps on Windows 11.
